title: [Chapitre] VII. Analysis situs (troisième mouture) : notes manuscrites (23-26/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: Grothendieck's 1986 'Analysis situs' notes build a pointless (point-free) topology on an 'atelier' F. An atelier is a set of 'figures' with an order ≤ (being a part of), a relation ≪ ('well inside', relatively compact or non-tangential inclusion), a symmetric relation ∥ (disjoint or separated), and a distinguished subfamily U of 'open' figures.

Page 61, 'Notion de support', does three things.

(1) Two families of subsets.
- Σ_F ⊂ P(F) is the set of subsets of F that are closed for ≪ (a ≪-rounded downward condition, with a parenthetical 'for ≤' whose wording is uncertain) and stable under arbitrary (finite or infinite) ≤-sups.
- Σ_U is the set of subsets of U closed for ≪.

(2) A claimed isomorphism of ordered sets, after which both sides are identified to a single poset Σ:
- Σ_F → Σ_U sends B to B ∩ U.
- Σ_U → Σ_F sends S to L_S = {F | F̂ ⊂ S}. Here F̂ is presumably the set of open figures attached to F, e.g. those ≪ F or containing F.
- In modern terms Σ plays the role of the frame or locale of 'open regions': rounded ideals of a base, as in the construction of a locale from a continuous lattice or proximity base.

(3) A Galois connection (polarity) from ∥.
- For A ⊂ F, cosupp A = {G | G ∥ F for all F ∈ A}, the figures 'disjoint from' all of A.
- A margin note introduces F ∥ A and A ∥ B, with the five equivalent formulations (A ⊂ cosupp B, B ⊂ cosupp A, and so on). These are equivalent trivially because ∥ is symmetric.
- Claim: cosupp A ∈ Σ_F.
- Then supp A (also written Ā) = cosupp(cosupp A). He warns that this is not the topological closure of A for the topologies on F defined by ≤ or ≪.
- He stresses that everything is formal and holds for any relation between two sets.

The next page lists the standard closure-operator properties:
- antitonicity of cosupp;
- extensivity, monotonicity and idempotence of the closure Ā;
- fixed points ('F-supports', forming Σ⁰_F) are exactly the cosupports;
- cosupp induces an involutive order-anti-isomorphism Σ⁰_F → Σ⁰_F.

In a space where ∥ means disjointness, A ↦ A^⊥⊥ corresponds to U ↦ int(cl U). So the supports are the regular-open regions and Σ⁰ is an orthocomplemented, generically Boolean, complete lattice. The purpose is to define the 'support' of a family of figures intrinsically from the atelier data, preparing a point-free notion of complement (∁A = cosupp A, page 62).
errors: The claim cosupp A ∈ Σ_F is not purely formal. Stability of cosupp A under arbitrary ≤-sups requires an axiom of the type (∀i, G_i ∥ F) ⇒ sup G_i ∥ F, i.e. infinite distributivity of disjointness over joins. Closure under ≪ requires G' ≪ G (or ≤ G) and G ∥ F ⇒ G' ∥ F. These must be atelier axioms; they are not consequences of the polarity alone.

Margin remark 'supp A ∩ supp B = ∅' for A ∥ B: as sets of figures this can only hold up to the empty/zero figure, which is ∥ to everything and lies in every cosupport. Strictly, the intersection is {0}, or the statement should be read as disjointness of the corresponding regions.
The bijection Σ_F ⇄ Σ_U is asserted without proof. It depends on unstated axioms, e.g. every figure being the sup of the open figures ≪ it, and on the precise definition of F̂.

ideas.what: Correspondence between ≪-closed, sup-stable families of figures and ≪-closed families of open figures (rounded ideals), identified to one poset Σ of 'regions'
ideas.modern_name: Rounded ideals / ideal completion of a proximity or continuous base; frame of opens of a locale presented by a base with a way-below relation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Scott and Gierz–Hofmann–Keimel–Lawson–Mislove–Scott (continuous lattices, 1970s–80); Johnstone, Stone Spaces (1982); de Vries (1962) for compingent algebras

ideas.what: Cosupport and support via the disjointness relation ∥: A ↦ A^∥, with supp A = A^∥∥
ideas.modern_name: Galois connection / Birkhoff polarity of a symmetric relation; orthogonality space; regular-open closure int(cl(·))
ideas.usually_credited_to: Birkhoff (Lattice Theory, 1940); orthogonality spaces (Foulis–Randall, Dacey, 1960s–70s); Wille's formal concept analysis (1982)

ideas.what: Point-free 'analysis situs' with primitive relations ≤ (part), ≪ (well-inside) and ∥ (disjoint) on a set of figures
ideas.modern_name: Mereotopology / region-based topology: contact algebras, de Vries proximity algebras, Region Connection Calculus
ideas.usually_credited_to: Whitehead (1929), de Laguna (1922), Tarski (geometry of solids, 1929), de Vries (1962), Clarke (1981), Randell–Cui–Cohn (1992), Dimov–Vakarelov (2006)
ideas.where_published: Analysis situs / 'ateliers' only in the unpublished Montpellier notes; tame-topology motivation appears in Esquisse d'un programme (1984)

missed.claim: Grothendieck's 'atelier' formalism (figures with ≤, ≪, ∥, open figures, supports as ∥∥-closed families) is an independent reinvention of region-based topology / contact and proximity algebras (de Vries, Whitehead–Tarski mereotopology). The literature on mereotopology and Grothendieck's 'tame topology' programme do not appear to have been connected.
missed.quote: cosupp A = {G ∈ F | ∀F ∈ A, F ∥ G} ... supp A = cosupp(cosupp A), il est formel (en termes de la seule donnée d'une relation ∥ dans l'ens. abstrait F
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It would link Grothendieck's tame-topology / analysis situs project (Esquisse) to an existing mathematical-logic tradition (contact algebras, de Vries duality, Stone-type dualities for regions). This might give a ready-made axiomatics and duality theory for his ateliers, and suggest o-minimal or polyhedral instances of contact algebras.

missed.claim: The page sets up the polarity-based support/complement on an atelier, but the axioms needed for cosupp A ∈ Σ_F, and the relation between Σ (≪-rounded regions) and Σ⁰ (∥∥-closed supports, i.e. regular regions), are left implicit.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Making this precise amounts to an inclusion of the Boolean algebra of regular regions into the frame of regions inside a tame/polyhedral point-free topology. That would be a small but concrete piece of a point-free foundation for tame topology.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics on the page is formal: a Galois connection from a symmetric relation plus rounded ideals, all classical. The mildly notable point is that Grothendieck builds a point-free, mereotopology-like framework (≤, ≪, ∥) for tame/polyhedral topology, apparently unaware of de Vries / contact algebras, and this framework is not in the published record.
transcription_corrections: Margin note: the image reads approximately 'Ne pas confondre Ā avec l'adhérence de A pour la topol. de F associée soit à ≤, soit à ≪ !' — the transcription is essentially right.
Line 'On a, quoi: M.D., que' reads better as 'On voit, grâce à : [axiome] M.D. [?], que : cosupp A ∈ Σ_F'. The 'M.D.' likely refers to a numbered axiom, not 'Q.E.D.'.
The parenthetical inserted above 'fermées' reads roughly '(c'est-à-dire[?] par ≤)', not clearly 'cofinales'; uncertain.

Lower-left margin: '(iii) ∀X∈A, ∀Y∈B, X∥Y' (the 'iiii' item) and 'Sous cette notation ... supp A ∩ supp B = ∅ [?]' are very uncertain; the text runs obliquely and partially reads '... (i.e. l'intersection ...)'.
